To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the regularity effect in past tense inflection is not reliable when past tense is generated from meaning and that a single-mechanisim model that incorporates distributed phonological and lexical semantic representations can simulate this effect.

1) the magnitude of the past-tense regularity effect depends on the nature of the input (form vs. meaning), 2) a single-mechanical account of verb inflection can reproduce this pattern, and 3) this pattern of findings is problematic for dual-mechanistic accounts of inflectional processing.

the regularity effect in the past tense generation task was no longer reliable in a condition in which the task required the participant to generate the past from meaning rather than form and this outcome would appear problematic to the extent that it is inconsistent with dual-mechanism models of verb inflection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the processing of regular and irregular past-tense verbs is sensitive to the nature of the task.
the relationship between the form and meaning of words, and the implications this relationship has for the way we think about language and its processing.
the nature of verb inflection and how it relates to the mental representations of words.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present study are not consistent with the dual-mechanism account of verb morphology.
the dual-mechanism theory of inflection is not supported by the evidence.
the results from this study are not consistent with the dual-mechanism account, and they are consistent with the single-mechanism account.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the task of generating the past tense from form is not the same task as generating the past tense when given a picture, and that the task of generation is sensitive to the task context in which it is embedded.
dual- and single-mechanisms theories are both viable in explaining verb inflection, but the latter is more consistent with the behavioural and modelling evidence.
the task of generating the past tense from a verb's stem is a reliable predictor of the magnitude of the past-tense regularity effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the processing advantage of regular over irregular inflections is task-dependent.
the task of past-tense generation influences the processing of regular and irregular verbs in ways that are difficult to explain within the dual-mechanism framework.
, in addition to the behavioural data, computational modelling provides a useful way to test the predictions of different theories.
